key_terms.meaning: Diode circuit that converts AC into pulsating DC by conducting in one direction only.
Maximum reverse voltage across an off diode in a rectifier.
r = V<sub>r(rms)</sub>/V<sub>DC</sub>, the AC ripple divided by the DC output.
Shunt capacitor that stores charge on peaks and releases it to reduce ripple.
Circuit that removes the part of a waveform above or below a chosen level.
Circuit that adds a DC shift to a waveform without changing its peak-to-peak value.
Reverse-biased diode that holds an almost constant voltage in breakdown.
Change in output voltage for a given change in input voltage.
Change in output voltage from no load to full load.
Transistor in series that drops excess input voltage to hold output steady.
Regulator that shunts excess current away from the load to hold voltage steady.
Amplifier that compares a feedback sample with a reference and drives the control device.
Minimum input-to-output difference needed for a linear regulator to regulate.
Protection that reduces output current sharply on overload.
Protection that turns off a regulator when chip temperature exceeds a safe limit.
Linear IC regulator that works with a small input-output difference.
D = T<sub>on</sub>/T, the fraction of switching period the switch is on.
Switching converter that steps voltage down.
Switching converter that steps voltage up.
Diode-capacitor network that gives DC at a multiple of the input peak.

takeaways: Rectifiers use diode one-way conduction to make pulsating DC; a bridge rectifier gives full-wave output without a centre tap.
A filter capacitor reduces ripple by storing energy, and ripple factor compares AC ripple with DC output.
Clippers cut off waveform peaks, while clampers shift the whole waveform in DC level without changing its shape.
A Zener regulator holds load voltage near V<sub>Z</sub> by shunting excess current when the input or load changes.
Series and shunt transistor regulators use feedback to reduce output changes caused by input and load variation.
IC regulators integrate a reference, error amplifier and pass device; 78xx and 79xx give fixed outputs and LM317 gives an adjustable output.
Linear regulators are simple and low-noise but waste power as heat when the input-output difference is large.
Switched-mode supplies chop at high frequency and control duty cycle for high efficiency and small size.
Voltage multipliers add capacitor voltages to produce about 2×, 3× or 4× the input peak for high-voltage low-current loads.
bank_note: Long answers usually demand a labelled circuit, input and output waveforms, the V<sub>DC</sub> and ripple formulas, and a clear comparison of linear and switching regulator choices.

bank.q: Draw and explain a half-wave rectifier. Derive its DC output voltage, ripple factor and peak inverse voltage.
outline: Half-wave circuit with one diode and load resistor.
Input and output waveforms.
V<sub>DC</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/π and I<sub>DC</sub> = I<sub>m</sub>/π.
Ripple factor r = 1.21.
PIV = V<sub>m</sub>.
Output frequency equals supply frequency.

bank.q: Compare centre-tapped full-wave and bridge rectifiers on diode count, PIV, transformer requirement and output frequency.
outline: Centre-tap uses two diodes; bridge uses four diodes.
Centre-tap needs a centre-tapped transformer; bridge does not.
PIV is 2V<sub>m</sub> for centre-tap and V<sub>m</sub> for bridge.
Both give ripple at 2f.
Bridge has two diode drops in the conduction path.

bank.q: Explain how a capacitor filter reduces ripple in a rectified supply. Define ripple factor and give its expression for a capacitor-filtered full-wave rectifier.
outline: Capacitor charges to peak and discharges through the load.
Smaller discharge gives smaller ripple.
Ripple factor r = V<sub>r(rms)</sub>/V<sub>DC</sub>.
For capacitor-filtered full-wave, r ≈ 1/(4√3 f C R<sub>L</sub>).
Larger C lowers ripple but raises peak diode current.

bank.q: Describe clipper and clamper circuits with waveforms. State the difference between limiting and DC level shifting.
outline: Clipper circuits use a diode and bias to cut peaks.
Positive and negative clipper waveforms.
Clamper uses diode, capacitor and resistor.
Clamper shifts DC level with peak-to-peak value unchanged.
Clipper changes amplitude; clamper changes average level.

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz transformer with 12 V rms secondary feeds a bridge rectifier and capacitor filter. Find peak output, DC output, ripple frequency and required PIV.
outline: Bridge has two diode drops in conduction.
V<sub>DC</sub> ≈ V<sub>m</sub> − 2V<sub>D</sub> for a capacitor filter.
Ripple frequency = 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.
PIV for bridge ≈ V<sub>m</sub>.
Choose diode current and voltage ratings with margin.

bank.q: Design a Zener shunt regulator for V<sub>out</sub> = 6.2 V, I<sub>L</sub> = 20 mA and V<sub>in</sub> = 12 V using a 6.2 V Zener. Find the series resistor and worst-case powers.
outline: R<sub>S</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)/(I<sub>Z</sub> + I<sub>L</sub>).
Choose I<sub>Z</sub> above the minimum Zener current.
P<sub>Z</sub> = V<sub>Z</sub>I<sub>Z</sub> and P<sub>RS</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>Z</sub>)²/R<sub>S</sub>.
Check I<sub>Z</sub> at maximum load and minimum input.
Use worst-case power ratings.

bank.q: In a series transistor regulator, V<sub>in</sub> = 15 V, V<sub>out</sub> = 9 V and I<sub>L</sub> = 0.5 A. Find pass transistor power loss and efficiency. Explain why a heat sink is needed.
outline: P<sub>pass</sub> = (V<sub>in</sub> − V<sub>out</sub>)I<sub>L</sub> = (15 − 9) × 0.5 = 3 W.
Efficiency ≈ V<sub>out</sub>/V<sub>in</sub> = 60%.
Heat sink keeps junction temperature safe.
Pass transistor operates in the active region.
Input and load variations are absorbed by the pass device.

bank.q: Using a 7805, draw a fixed 5 V supply from a 12 V input. Add a capacitor filter and calculate the minimum dropout requirement and power dissipated at 0.7 A.
outline: 7805 pinout and input/output capacitors.
Dropout is about 2 V; 12 V input leaves 7 V across the regulator.
Heat sink and filter capacitor are needed.
Output is fixed at 5 V.

bank.q: Analyze a capacitor-filtered full-wave rectifier and explain how load resistance and filter capacitance affect ripple and diode current.
outline: Ripple decreases as C and R<sub>L</sub> increase.
Load current discharges the capacitor faster.
Diode current pulses are narrow and large.
Ripple frequency is 2f for full-wave.
Trade-off between low ripple and high diode stress.

bank.q: Compare linear and switched-mode power supplies for a 5 V, 2 A phone charger. Discuss efficiency, size, noise and thermal design.
outline: Linear supply is simple and low-noise but inefficient at large dropout.
SMPS is efficient and small but has switching noise and EMI.
For 5 V 2 A, linear loss is (V<sub>in</sub> − 5) × 2 W.
SMPS uses inductor or transformer and duty-cycle control.
Thermal design and heat sinking differ.
Choice depends on cost, size, noise and input voltage.

bank.q: A Zener regulator must supply a load that varies from 0 to 50 mA while input varies by ±10%. Analyze whether the Zener stays in breakdown and select component ratings.
outline: Zener current must stay between I<sub>Z(min)</sub> and I<sub>Z(max)</sub>.
Worst case is low input with high load.
R<sub>S</sub> is set from minimum Zener current.
Check maximum Zener current at high input and no load.
Select Zener and resistor power ratings.
Discuss line and load regulation.

bank.q: Evaluate buck, boost and buck-boost converters for battery-powered equipment. Explain duty-cycle control and losses.
outline: Buck steps down, boost steps up, buck-boost inverts.
Duty cycle sets output voltage.
Inductor stores and transfers energy.
Losses include conduction, switching, inductor and capacitor ESR.
Efficiency affects battery life.
Input current pulsation and noise matter.

bank.q: Design and compare a voltage doubler and a bridge rectifier for a high-voltage low-current application. Include PIV, capacitor rating and ripple.
outline: Doubler uses two diodes and two capacitors.
Doubler output ≈ 2V<sub>m</sub>; PIV ≈ 2V<sub>m</sub>.
Bridge gives full-wave output but no multiplication.
Capacitor voltage ratings must exceed peak stress.
Ripple and load regulation are poorer at high load.
Doubler suits high-voltage low-current loads.

glossary.def: Current that reverses direction periodically.
Current that flows in one direction.
Two-terminal PN junction device that conducts mainly in one direction.
Circuit that converts AC to pulsating DC.
DC that varies in magnitude but not in direction.
Maximum reverse voltage a diode must withstand when off.
AC variation superimposed on rectified DC.
Ratio of ripple rms voltage to DC output voltage.
Network that reduces ripple in a rectified supply.
Shunt capacitor that stores charge and smooths output.
Circuit that removes part of a waveform.
Circuit that shifts a waveform's DC level.
Diode designed to operate safely in reverse breakdown.
Shunt regulator using a Zener diode to hold load voltage.
Change in output for a change in input voltage.
Change in output for a change in load current.
Linear regulator with a pass transistor in series with the load.
Linear regulator that shunts excess current away from the load.
Amplifier that compares feedback with a reference.
Minimum input-output difference for a linear regulator.
Linear regulator with small dropout voltage.
On-time divided by switching period in a switching converter.
Supply that switches at high frequency and regulates by duty cycle.
Diode-capacitor circuit giving a multiple of peak input voltage.
Measure of how little supply variation reaches the output.
Protection that turns off a regulator at excessive temperature.
